background.definition: The classic triad of normal-pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) includes gait abnormalities, dementia of the subcortical type, and urinary incontinence associated with enlarged ventricles on imaging and normal opening pressure during lumbar puncture (LP).

list.listitem: NPH is difficult to identify because of the lack of consensus for diagnostic criteria.
NPH accounts for approximately 5% of patients diagnosed with dementia.
NPH is equally common in men and women.

A systematic review found crude overall prevalence of 10 to 22/100,000 for probable idiopathic NPH and 29/100,000 for possible NPH. Prevalence varied by age, and was 3.3/100,000 in persons aged 50-59 years but 5.9% in persons 80 years and older.
Idiopathic NPH: unknown cause, strongly associated with hypertension and advancing age.
Secondary NPH: known cause, including fibrosis from a stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, or trauma.
NPH is usually due to impaired absorption of CSF, which causes increased pressure to various parts of the brain.
This in turn causes gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, and dementia.
Suspect normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) in any adult patient presenting with an insidious onset of gait disturbance, cognitive impairments, and/or urinary incontinence. C
MRI of the head, with or without contrast, is the most appropriate neuroimaging study for patients with suspected NPH. C

Routine spinal tap with an opening pressure of less than 200 mm of water with the patient in the left lateral recumbent position is consistent with the diagnosis of NPH if other diagnostic criteria met. C

Differential.Differential_Name: Senile dementia of the Alzheimer type
Differential.Differential_Features: More likely to have agnosia, apraxia
More likely to have word finding difficulty, as well as a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or hypercholesterolemia
More likely to have stooped gait, retropulsion, tremor, narrow-based gait
Likely to have other CNS effects

Differential.Differential_Name: Combination of spinal stenosis and dementia
Differential.Differential_Features: Needs a careful history and neurophysiological testing
More likely to have psychotic features
Would complain of neuropathic pain to explain gait abnormalities

list.listitem: Suspect NPH in any adult patient presenting with an insidious onset of gait disturbance, cognitive impairments, and/or urinary incontinence. Have a higher index of suspicion for secondary NPH in patients with a history of hypertension, meningitis, stroke, or trauma. It may be difficult to diagnose NPH because these symptoms are relatively common in the elderly.

History should be obtained from the patient and an informant, as cognitive impairments may make it difficult for the patient to provide an accurate history. Chronic, slow onset of symptoms that are commonly present for at least 3 months is typical.

Gait apraxia represents the first presenting symptom, usually described as a "magnetic gait" with decreased step height and length, as well as turning "en bloc." Other gait disturbances include difficulty with climbing stairs, walking at the expected pace, rising from a chair, "give-way" weakness of the legs, or fatigue with walking.

Urinary symptoms include frequency and urgency early on, with progression to incontinence with disease progression. However, recognize that urinary incontinence may never occur with NPH or may occur intermittently.
The primary cognitive symptoms of NPH include slowing of thought, difficulty with recall, lack of attentiveness, and apathy.
Seizures, headache, and papilledema at presentation are not expected signs and symptoms of NPH; consider other diagnoses when they are present.

MRI of the head, with or without contrast, is the recommended initial neuroimaging study for patients with suspected NPH followed by noncontrast CT brain imaging. Ventricular enlargement is diagnosed by an Evans Index of 0.3 (an increased ratio of ventricular size to the diameter of the cranium, calculated by the ratio of the maximum width of the frontal horns divided by the maximum distance of the inner tables of the skull on the transverse plane).
The splenial callosal angle on MRI correlates uniquely with gait, cognition in idiopathic NPH, and aids in distinguishing it from other neurological diseases.

Routine spinal tap with an opening pressure of less than 200 mm of water with the patient in the left lateral recumbent position is consistent with the diagnosis of NPH if other diagnostic criteria met.
A key step in the assessment of NPH is differentiating between patients likely to improve with shunt placement (shunt-responsive NPH and shunt-nonresponsive NPH). See .

Drainage of 40 to 50 mL of CSF and monitoring gait before and after the tap is thought to be useful for identifying those who might benefit from shunting. The reported sensitivity is 26% to 61% for identifying such patients. The positive predictive value of this maneuver is between 73% and 100% and the negative predictive value is between 23% and 42%. Therefore, recognize that many patients who might benefit from shunting may be missed with this test.

Continuous CSF drainage (720 mL more than 3 days) increases the sensitivity and the positive and negative predictive values in identifying shunt-responsive patients; however, this is invasive and requires inpatient hospitalization. Measurement of outflow resistance of CSF is also useful, especially if LP results are equivocal or negative.
More studies are needed assessing the diagnostic value of extended lumbar drainage for idiopathic NPH.
Continuous monitoring of intracranial pressure to document spikes of high pressure is not recommended.
The measurement of CSF flow velocities using MRI has low diagnostic value and is not currently recommended in the assessment of NPH.
Isotope cisternography that examines the rate of absorption of CSF has not proven useful in identifying NPH responsiveness to shunt therapy.
CSF biomarkers of neuronal degeneration (eg, elevated levels of neurofilament protein light, and lower levels of hyperphosphorylated tau and beta-amyloid 1-42) have been seen in NPH.
Suspect NPH in patients with gait disturbance, dementia, and/or urinary incontinence. All 3 components of the classic triad need not be present to make the diagnosis of NPH.
Order MRI, with or without contrast, to confirm the diagnosis. CT without contrast is an alternative.

On the basis of clinical and neuroimaging, categorize patient as either probable, possible, or unlikely to have idiopathic NPH (). All probable and possible NPH patients should be considered for supplemental testing. If diagnosis is not confirmed by MRI but cannot be ruled out, consider additional testing (CSF outflow resistance, LP, and external lumbar drainage).

There are no randomized trials on the effectiveness of shunting for NPH.
Antibiotic prophylaxis for the first 24 hours following shunt insertion (OR = 0.52) and use of antibiotic-impregnated shunts (OR = 0.21) reduce the risk of infection.

Ventriculoperitoneal shunting is associated with variable success rates (33%-90% more than 1 year or less of follow-up), depending on the study and the definition of NPH with the most improvement with gait.

Twelve-month improvement in gait (90%), cognition (77%), and urinary continence (62%) was noted in shunted patients who demonstrated improvement with the CSF tap test or external CSF drainage. Short-term and long-term outcomes of shunting are a function of the selection of patients, the postoperative assessment techniques, and the duration of follow-up.

Long-term complications of shunting include subdural fluid collections such as hygromas and hematomas (2%-17%), shunt infection (3%-6%), seizures (3%-11%), and less commonly hearing loss, tinnitus, oculomotor palsies, and headache.
Shunt revision rate is 21% after 5 years, and shunt-related mortality is 2%.

An observational study with 132 patients concluded that those with reduced gray matter volume in the supplementary motor area and posterior parietal cortex were less likely to respond favorable to CSF drainage.
Anyone with the classic triad of gait abnormality, dementia, and urinary incontinence and CT or MRI of the brain with enlarged ventricles should be evaluated by a neurologist and/or a neurosurgeon.

The Framingham Risk Score is recommended to predict short-term and 10-year mortality risk in patients with idiopathic NPH. B

feature.caption: Identifying Shunt-Responsive Idiopathic NPH Patients.
feature.feature_body:
Step 1 Clinical and neuroimaging evaluation consistent with probable or possible NPH: proceed to supplemental testing.
Step 2 CSF tap test can be performed on an outpatient basis. Proceed with the CSF tap test by removing 40 to 50 mL of CSF. If a favorable clinical response is noted, the predictive value for a positive response to shunting is 72% to 100%. If no improvement in clinical response is noted, order additional supplemental testing.
Step 3 Resistance testing (CSF Ro, which measures impedance to CSF flow through its absorption pathways) can be performed on an outpatient basis. Infuse fluid, such as saline, into the subarachnoid space with subsequent measurements (eg, ICP recording). Sensitivity for identifying shunt-responsive NPH is 57% to 100%.
Step 4 External lumbar drainage (ELD) requires a hospital admission for the slow removal of CSF (10 mL per hour) for several days, with 300 to 720 mL CSF removed. The sensitivity of this procedure is 50% to 100% and the positive predictive value is 80% to 100%. ELD has a higher complication rate than other studies.
Data from Marmarou A, Bergsneider M, Klinge P, Relkin N, Black PM. The value of supplemental prognostic tests for the preoperative assessment of idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Neurosurgery 2005;57:S17-S28; discussion ii-v.

feature.caption: Description of Idiopathic Normal-Pressure Hydrocephalus Classification: Probable, Possible, and Unlikely Categories.*
feature.feature_body:
Probable INPH: The diagnosis of probable INPH is based on clinical history, brain imaging, physical findings, and physiological criteria. History: Reported symptoms should be corroborated by an informant familiar with the patient's premorbid and current condition, and must include Insidious onset (versus acute) Origin after age 40 y A minimum duration of at least 3 to 6 mo No evidence of an antecedent event such as head trauma, intracerebral hemorrhage, meningitis, or other known causes of secondary hydrocephalus Progression over time No other neurological, psychiatric, or general medical conditions that are sufficient to explain the presenting symptoms
Brain imaging: A brain imaging study (CT or MRI) performed after onset of symptoms must show evidence ofOther brain imaging findings may be supportive of an INPH diagnosis but are not required for a "Probable" designation Ventricular enlargement not entirely attributable to cerebral atrophy or congenital enlargement (Evan's index >0.3 or comparable measure) No macroscopic obstruction to CSF flow At least one of the following supportive features Enlargement of the temporal horns of the lateral ventricles not entirely attributable to hippocampus atrophy Callosal angle of 40° or more Evidence of altered brain water content, including periventricular signal changes on CT and MRI not attributable to microvascular ischemic changes or demyelination An aqueductal or fourth ventricular flow void on MRI
Clinical: By classic definitions (Fisher [17], Hakim [22], etc.), findings of gait/balance disturbance must be present, plus at least one other area of impairment in cognition, urinary symptoms, or both. With respect to gait/balance, at least 2 of the following should be present and not be entirely attributable to other conditionsWith respect to cognition, there must be documented impairment (adjusted for age and educational attainment) and/or decrease in performance on a cognitive screening instrument (such as the Monumental State examination), or evidence of at least two of the following on examination that is not fully attributable to other conditions To document symptoms in the domain of urinary continence, either one of the following should be present Or any 2 of the following should be present Decreased step height Decreased step length Decreased cadence (speed of walking) Increased trunk sway during walking Widened standing base Toes turned outward on walking Retropulsion (spontaneous or provoked) En bloc turning (turning requiring 3 or more steps for 180°) Impaired walking balance, as evidenced by 2 or more corrections out of 8 steps on tandem gait testing
Physiological CSF opening pressure in the range of 5 to 18 mm Hg (or 70-245 mm H2O) as determined by a lumbar puncture or a comparable procedure. Appropriately measured pressures that are significantly higher or lower than this range are not consistent with a probable NPH diagnosis.
History: Reported symptoms may Have a subacute or indeterminate mode of onset Begin at any age after childhood May have less than 3 mo or indeterminate duration May follow events such as mild head trauma, remote history of intracerebral hemorrhage, or childhood and adolescent meningitis or other conditions that in the judgment of the clinician are not likely to be causally related Coexist with other neurological, psychiatric, or general medical disorders but in the judgment of the clinician not be entirely attributable to these conditions Be nonprogressive or not clearly progressive
Brain imaging: Ventricular enlargement consistent with hydrocephalus but associated with any of the following Evidence of cerebral atrophy of sufficient severity to potentially explain ventricular size Structural lesions that may influence ventricular size
Clinical: Symptoms of either Incontinence and/or cognitive impairment in the absence of an observable gait or balance disturbance Gait disturbance or dementia alone
Physiological: Opening pressure measurement not available or pressure outside the range required for probable INPH. Unlikely INPH No evidence of ventriculomegaly Signs of increased intracranial pressure such as papilledema No component of the clinical triad of INPH is present Symptoms explained by other causes (eg, spinal stenosis)
*INPH, idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus; CT, computed tomography; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging; CSF, cerebrospinal fluid; SPECT, single-photon emission computed tomography. From Relkin N, Marmarou A, Klinge P, Bergsneider M, Black PM. Diagnosing idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Neurosurgery 2005;57:S4-S16; discussion ii-v. Possible: INPHA diagnosis of possible INPH is based on historical, brain imaging, and clinical and physiological criteria.
